topics.title: Python Syntax, Variables & Data Types
topics.summary: Python's dynamic typing model and the core built-in types used in almost every program.
keyPoints: Dynamic typing: variables are references to objects, not fixed-type storage
Core types: int, float, str, bool, and Python 3's arbitrary-precision integers
Mutable vs immutable types (list/dict/set are mutable; tuple/str/int are immutable)
Indentation-based blocks instead of braces

interviewQA.question: What does it mean that Python is 'dynamically typed', and what's the trade-off?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: In Python, a variable is just a name bound to an object, and its type is determined by the object it currently references, checked at runtime rather than compile time. This gives huge flexibility and less boilerplate, but it means type errors surface only when the code actually runs, and IDEs/readers have less static information. Python 3.5+ added optional type hints (PEP 484) to get some of the benefits of static typing via tools like mypy, without changing the runtime behavior.
interviewQA.tip: Mention type hints and mypy as the modern middle ground.

topics.title: Control Flow & Functions
topics.summary: Conditionals, loops, and defining reusable functions with Python's flexible argument system.
keyPoints: if/elif/else, for (with range/enumerate), while, and Python 3.10+ match statement
Function definitions with default args, *args, **kwargs
First-class functions: passing functions as arguments, returning them
Scope rules: LEGB (Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in)

interviewQA.question: What's the danger of using a mutable default argument in a Python function?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Default argument values are evaluated once at function definition time, not on every call. If you use a mutable default like def f(x, lst=[]), that same list object is reused and mutated across every call that doesn't pass its own list, causing unexpected shared state between calls. The standard fix is to default to None and create a new list inside the function body if it's None.
interviewQA.tip: Give the classic def append_to(x, lst=[]) example to demonstrate the bug.

topics.title: Lists, Tuples, Dicts & Sets
topics.summary: Python's built-in collection types, their performance characteristics, and idiomatic usage.
keyPoints: List: ordered, mutable, O(1) index access, O(n) search
Tuple: ordered, immutable, hashable if contents are hashable
Dict: hash map, insertion-ordered since Python 3.7, O(1) average lookup
Set: unordered unique elements, O(1) average membership check

interviewQA.question: When would you choose a tuple over a list, beyond just 'tuples are immutable'?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Because tuples are immutable and hashable (as long as their elements are), they can be used as dictionary keys or set members, which lists cannot. Tuples also signal intent — a fixed-size, heterogeneous record like (x, y) coordinates — versus a list which implies a homogeneous, resizable collection. Tuples are also slightly more memory-efficient and faster to create than lists.
interviewQA.tip: Lead with the hashability/dictionary-key point — that's the concrete technical difference.

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.summary: Python's try/except model for handling errors gracefully, using EAFP-style code.
keyPoints: try/except/else/finally and catching specific exception types
Custom exceptions by subclassing Exception
EAFP ('easier to ask forgiveness than permission') vs LBYL ('look before you leap')
Context managers (with statement) for guaranteed cleanup

interviewQA.question: What is the EAFP coding style in Python and why is it preferred over LBYL?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: EAFP means you attempt the operation directly inside a try block and handle the exception if it fails, rather than checking preconditions first (LBYL, e.g. checking 'if key in dict' before accessing it). EAFP is preferred in Python partly for style and partly for correctness: checking then acting can introduce race conditions in concurrent code, since the state could change between the check and the action. It's also often faster when the exceptional case is rare, since exceptions are relatively cheap in Python compared to repeated condition checks.
interviewQA.tip: Use dict key access or file existence as a concrete example.

topics.title: String Manipulation & Formatting
topics.summary: Working with text data efficiently using Python's rich string toolkit.
keyPoints: f-strings are the modern, readable way to format strings: f'{name} is {age}'
Common methods: split, join, strip, replace, startswith/endswith
Strings are immutable, so methods return new strings rather than modifying in place
Slicing (s[1:5], s[::-1]) is a powerful, Pythonic way to extract or reverse text

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between str.split() and str.split(',') on a string with multiple spaces?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: str.split() with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and discards empty strings, which is usually what you want for free-form text. str.split(',') splits on the literal comma character only, so consecutive commas produce empty strings in the result — important for CSV-like data.
interviewQA.tip: Give a quick example: 'a  b'.split() -> ['a','b'] vs 'a,,b'.split(',') -> ['a','','b'].

topics.title: Working with JSON & APIs (requests)
topics.summary: Consuming and producing JSON, the universal data format for talking to web APIs.
keyPoints: json.loads()/json.dumps() convert between JSON text and Python dict/list
The requests library: requests.get(url, params=...) and response.json()
Always check response.status_code / raise_for_status() before trusting the payload
Handle timeouts and exceptions — a network call can always fail

interviewQA.question: Why should you always set a timeout on a requests call in production code?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Without a timeout, requests will wait indefinitely if the remote server is slow or unresponsive, which can hang your whole application or exhaust a thread/connection pool. Always pass timeout=(connect, read) so a slow dependency fails fast instead of cascading.
interviewQA.tip: Mention retry logic with backoff as a natural follow-up for flaky APIs.

topics.title: Object-Oriented Programming in Python
topics.summary: Classes, inheritance, and Python-specific OOP mechanics like dunder methods and properties.
keyPoints: class definitions, __init__, self, and instance vs class attributes
Inheritance and method resolution order (MRO) with multiple inheritance
Dunder methods (__str__, __eq__, __len__) for operator overloading
@property for computed attributes with getter/setter semantics

interviewQA.question: How does Python resolve method calls when a class has multiple inheritance, and what is MRO?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Python uses the C3 linearization algorithm to compute the Method Resolution Order — a consistent, predictable order in which base classes are searched for an attribute or method. You can inspect it via ClassName.__mro__. This resolves the 'diamond problem': if two parent classes share a common ancestor, C3 ensures each class appears once and before its own parents, so calling super() in each class's __init__ cooperatively chains through the whole hierarchy correctly.
interviewQA.tip: Mention ClassName.__mro__ as a way to actually inspect the order.

topics.title: Modules, Packages & Virtual Environments
topics.summary: Organizing code into reusable modules/packages and isolating project dependencies.
keyPoints: Modules (.py files) vs packages (directories with __init__.py)
import mechanics, sys.path, and relative vs absolute imports
Virtual environments (venv) to isolate per-project dependencies
requirements.txt / pyproject.toml and pip for dependency management

interviewQA.question: Why do we use virtual environments in Python projects?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A virtual environment creates an isolated Python installation with its own site-packages directory, so each project can install the exact package versions it needs without conflicting with other projects or the system Python. Without it, two projects needing different versions of the same library would clash on a single global installation, and upgrading one project's dependency could silently break another. Tools like venv, virtualenv, or poetry manage this isolation and let you pin exact versions via requirements.txt or pyproject.toml.
interviewQA.tip: Give a concrete example: Project A needs Django 3, Project B needs Django 4.

topics.title: File Handling & Context Managers
topics.summary: Reading/writing files safely and building custom context managers for resource management.
keyPoints: open() modes (r, w, a, b) and always using 'with' for automatic closing
Context manager protocol: __enter__ / __exit__
contextlib.contextmanager decorator for a simpler generator-based approach
Working with JSON/CSV via the standard library

interviewQA.question: How would you write a custom context manager, and why is it better than a try/finally block?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: You implement __enter__ (setup, returns the resource) and __exit__ (cleanup, receives exception info if one occurred) on a class, or use @contextlib.contextmanager to write it as a generator function with a single yield separating setup from teardown. It's not strictly 'better' than try/finally, but it's more reusable and readable — the cleanup logic is defined once and reused everywhere with 'with', rather than duplicated across every call site, and it composes cleanly with multiple resources in one with statement.
interviewQA.tip: Mention the @contextmanager decorator as the quick, Pythonic way to build one.

topics.title: Decorators & Generators
topics.summary: Two of Python's signature features: wrapping functions with decorators and lazy iteration with generators.
keyPoints: Decorators as higher-order functions that wrap behavior (logging, caching, auth checks)
functools.wraps to preserve metadata of the wrapped function
Generators (yield) for lazy, memory-efficient iteration over large/infinite sequences
Generator expressions vs list comprehensions

interviewQA.question: What's the difference between a generator and a regular function that returns a list, and when does it matter?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: A regular function computes the entire result and returns it as one object in memory; a generator function uses 'yield' to produce values one at a time, pausing its state between calls, so the full sequence is never materialized at once. This matters enormously for large or infinite sequences — processing a huge file line by line with a generator uses constant memory, while reading it all into a list could exhaust RAM. The trade-off is you can only iterate a generator once, and you lose random access (no indexing).
interviewQA.tip: Use processing a multi-GB file line by line as the motivating example.

topics.title: Testing with Pytest & Unittest
topics.summary: Writing maintainable, fast tests that catch regressions before they reach production.
keyPoints: pytest uses plain assert statements and fixtures (@pytest.fixture) for setup/teardown
Parametrized tests (@pytest.mark.parametrize) run the same logic against many inputs
unittest.mock.patch replaces real dependencies (APIs, DB calls) with controllable fakes
Aim for fast, isolated unit tests plus a smaller set of integration tests

interviewQA.question: How would you test a function that calls an external payment API, without actually calling it?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Use unittest.mock.patch (or pytest's monkeypatch) to replace the API client with a mock object, configure its return value or side_effect to simulate success/failure responses, and assert your function behaves correctly for each case — all without any real network call.
interviewQA.tip: Mention testing both the happy path and an error/timeout path from the mocked dependency.

topics.title: Type Hints & Static Typing (mypy)
topics.summary: Adding optional static types to Python for better tooling, fewer bugs, and self-documenting code.
keyPoints: Basic syntax: def add(a: int, b: int) -> int; variables: count: int = 0
Optional[T] / T | None for values that can be None; List[T], Dict[K, V] for containers
mypy is a static checker that runs separately — types are not enforced at runtime by default
Type hints improve IDE autocomplete and catch mismatched-type bugs before code runs

interviewQA.question: Since Python doesn't enforce type hints at runtime, what's the actual value of adding them?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Type hints act as machine-checked documentation: a static checker like mypy can catch a whole class of bugs (passing a str where an int is expected) before the code ever runs, and IDEs use them for accurate autocomplete and refactoring safety — even though Python itself ignores them at runtime.
interviewQA.tip: Note that libraries like pydantic DO enforce types at runtime, which is a related but different mechanism.

topics.title: Concurrency: GIL, Threading & Asyncio
topics.summary: How Python handles parallel and concurrent work, and the constraints imposed by the Global Interpreter Lock.
keyPoints: GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time
threading module: good for I/O-bound work despite the GIL (I/O releases the GIL)
multiprocessing: true parallelism for CPU-bound work via separate processes
asyncio: single-threaded cooperative concurrency for high-throughput I/O-bound workloads

interviewQA.question: Given the GIL, how would you speed up a CPU-bound Python task versus an I/O-bound one?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: For CPU-bound work (heavy computation), threading won't help because the GIL prevents true parallel bytecode execution — instead use multiprocessing, which spawns separate processes each with its own interpreter and GIL, achieving real parallelism across CPU cores at the cost of higher memory usage and IPC overhead. For I/O-bound work (network calls, file/database access), threading works fine because the GIL is released during I/O waits, or better, use asyncio for very high-concurrency I/O since it avoids thread context-switching overhead entirely with an event loop and coroutines.
interviewQA.tip: Be precise: threading helps I/O-bound, multiprocessing helps CPU-bound, asyncio scales I/O-bound further.

topics.title: Django & Flask Web Frameworks
topics.summary: Building web applications and APIs with Python's two most common frameworks, and when to choose each.
keyPoints: Django: batteries-included (ORM, admin, auth, migrations) — good for larger, structured apps
Flask: minimal microframework, add only what you need — good for APIs and smaller services
Django ORM QuerySets, migrations, and the MTV (Model-Template-View) pattern
Flask extensions (Flask-SQLAlchemy, Flask-RESTful) for building up functionality

interviewQA.question: How would you decide between Django and Flask for a new project?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: Django is a good fit when you need a full-featured app quickly — built-in admin panel, ORM, authentication, and a strong 'convention over configuration' structure that scales well across a team, especially for content-heavy or CRUD-heavy applications. Flask is better when you want fine-grained control over architecture, are building a lightweight API or microservice, or want to hand-pick libraries (e.g., a specific ORM or serializer) rather than accept Django's defaults. Many teams also use FastAPI now for high-performance async APIs with automatic OpenAPI docs, which sits between the two in philosophy.
interviewQA.tip: It's fine to mention FastAPI as a modern third option interviewers may probe on.

topics.title: Data Science with Pandas & NumPy
topics.summary: Vectorized numerical computation and tabular data manipulation, the foundation of Python's data science stack.
keyPoints: NumPy ndarrays: contiguous typed memory, vectorized operations avoid slow Python loops
Pandas DataFrame/Series built on NumPy, with labeled indices and missing-data handling
Vectorization vs apply() vs iterrows() performance trade-offs
Broadcasting rules for operating on arrays of different shapes

interviewQA.question: Why is a NumPy array operation typically much faster than an equivalent Python for-loop?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: NumPy stores array data in contiguous, fixed-type memory blocks (unlike Python lists, which store pointers to scattered objects), and its operations are implemented in compiled C code that can use vectorized CPU instructions (SIMD) to process multiple elements per instruction. A Python for-loop, by contrast, incurs interpreter overhead and dynamic type checking on every single iteration. This is why 'vectorizing' code — replacing explicit loops with NumPy/Pandas operations — is one of the biggest performance wins in data science code.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that Pandas' apply() is often not much faster than a loop — true vectorized ops are the real win.

topics.title: Performance Optimization & Cython
topics.summary: Profiling and speeding up Python code when pure-Python performance isn't enough.
keyPoints: Profiling first (cProfile, line_profiler) before optimizing blindly
Algorithmic improvements usually beat micro-optimizations
Cython / C extensions to compile hot paths to native code
Caching with functools.lru_cache for expensive repeated computations

interviewQA.question: A Python function is running too slowly in production. Walk through your approach to fixing it.
interviewQA.modelAnswer: First, profile before guessing — use cProfile or py-spy to find the actual bottleneck rather than assuming. Often the fix is algorithmic: replacing an O(n^2) approach with a hash-based O(n) one, or eliminating redundant recomputation with functools.lru_cache. If the bottleneck is genuinely CPU-bound Python overhead in a tight loop, consider vectorizing with NumPy, rewriting the hot path in Cython or using a library like Numba for JIT compilation, or as a last resort, moving that piece into a compiled extension or a different service.
interviewQA.tip: Always start the answer with 'profile first' — that's what interviewers want to hear.

topics.title: FastAPI & Modern API Development
topics.summary: Building high-performance, self-documenting REST APIs using Python type hints.
keyPoints: Path/query parameters and request bodies are declared via type-hinted function signatures
Pydantic models validate and serialize request/response data automatically
FastAPI auto-generates OpenAPI/Swagger docs from your type hints
Built on Starlette/ASGI, so it supports async def endpoints natively for high concurrency

interviewQA.question: Why is FastAPI able to handle more concurrent requests than a traditional sync Flask app for I/O-bound endpoints?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: FastAPI runs on ASGI with an async event loop, so an endpoint awaiting a database or API call yields control back to the loop instead of blocking a worker thread; a sync WSGI app like classic Flask ties up a whole worker/thread per in-flight request, so I/O-bound throughput is much lower per resource.
interviewQA.tip: Note that CPU-bound work still won't benefit from async — that still needs multiprocessing.

topics.title: Packaging, Deployment & Docker for Python Apps
topics.summary: Turning a Python project into something reliably deployable, from dependency pinning to containers.
keyPoints: pyproject.toml + a lockfile (poetry.lock/requirements.txt with pinned versions) for reproducible installs
Virtual environments isolate project dependencies from the system Python
A multi-stage Dockerfile keeps the final image slim by discarding build-only tools
Use a production WSGI/ASGI server (gunicorn + uvicorn workers), never the dev server, in production

interviewQA.question: Why shouldn't you run Flask's or FastAPI's built-in development server in production?
interviewQA.modelAnswer: The built-in dev server is single-threaded/single-process by default, has no proper process management, and isn't hardened for concurrent production traffic. A production ASGI/WSGI server like gunicorn with multiple uvicorn workers handles concurrency, worker restarts, and graceful shutdowns properly.
interviewQA.tip: Mention that debug mode in dev servers can also leak stack traces, which is a security risk in prod.
